cards.front: When do you use the preterite in Spanish?
cards.back:
Use the preterite for completed past actions with a definite start/end — the main narrative tense for storytelling.
Examples: El dragón atacó. Encontramos el tesoro. Jeffrey lanzó el hechizo.
cards.grammarNote: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) is the go-to tense for D&D storytelling — each completed action in the adventure is in the preterite. Contrast with the imperfect (pretérito imperfecto), which describes ongoing states or background conditions.

cards.front:
Preterite endings for regular -AR verbs
(e.g. atacar → but note spelling change!)
cards.back:
-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron
tirar: tiré, tiraste, tiró, tiramos, tirasteis, tiraron
lanzar (yo): lancé (z→c before e)
cards.grammarNote: -AR verbs add these endings to the stem. Key spelling changes in the yo form: c→qu (atacar → ataqué), z→c (lanzar → lancé), g→gu (llegar → llegué). Other persons are regular.

cards.front:
Preterite endings for regular -ER/-IR verbs
(e.g. comer, subir)
cards.back:
-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron
comer: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron
subir: subí, subiste, subió, subimos, subisteis, subieron
cards.grammarNote: -ER and -IR verbs share the same preterite endings. Note: -IR stem-changing verbs (e→i, o→u) apply the stem change in the él/ella and ellos forms only: **pedir → pidió, pidieron** (not in yo/tú/nosotros).

cards.front:
The dragon attacked the party.
(preterite narrative)
cards.grammarNote: **atacó** = he/she/it attacked — él/ella preterite of **atacar** (regular, no spelling change in third person). The yo form has the spelling change: **ataqué** (c→qu before e).

**Encontramos** = we found — nosotros preterite of **encontrar** (regular -ar). Note: the nosotros preterite of -ar verbs is identical to the nosotros present: **encontramos** = we find / we found. Context determines the tense.

cards.front:
Jeffrey cast a fire spell.
(preterite narrative)
cards.back: Jeffrey lanzó un hechizo de fuego.
cards.grammarNote: **lanzó** = he cast/threw — él/ella preterite of **lanzar** (regular in third person). The yo form has spelling change: **lancé** (z→c before e).

cards.front:
Preterite of SER (to be) and IR (to go)
[they share the same forms!]
cards.back:
fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
(same for both SER and IR — context clarifies meaning)
cards.grammarNote: **Fue** can mean 'he was' (ser) or 'he went' (ir) — only context tells you which. D&D examples: **El dragón fue derrotado** (The dragon was defeated — ser/passive) vs **El grupo fue a la mazmorra** (The group went to the dungeon — ir).

cards.back: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
cards.grammarNote: **hacer** has a completely irregular preterite. Note: **hizo** (él/ella form) uses z instead of c to preserve the soft /s/ sound before o. D&D context: **Jeffrey hizo un golpe crítico** (Jeffrey made a critical hit). **¿Qué hiciste?** (What did you do?)

cards.back: tuve, tuviste, tuvo, tuvimos, tuvisteis, tuvieron
cards.grammarNote: **tener** in the preterite often means 'got/obtained' rather than just 'had': **Tuve suerte** (I got lucky / I was lucky). D&D context: **Tuvimos éxito en la misión** (We succeeded in the quest — we had success).

cards.front: Preterite of PODER (to be able to)
cards.back: pude, pudiste, pudo, pudimos, pudisteis, pudieron
cards.grammarNote: **poder** in the preterite means 'managed to' (succeeded in doing something). D&D: **El explorador pudo disparar antes de que el dragón atacara** (The ranger managed to shoot before the dragon attacked).

cards.front:
The goblin died after two hits.
(-IR stem-changing verb in preterite)
cards.back: El duende murió después de dos golpes.
cards.grammarNote: **murió** = he/she died — preterite of **morir** (o→u stem change in él/ella and ellos preterite forms only): morí, moriste, **murió**, morimos, moristeis, **murieron**. This o→u shift applies to **-IR** verbs with o→ue or o→u in the present.

cards.front:
Jeffrey asked his brother to roll initiative.
(-IR e→i verb in preterite)
cards.back: Jeffrey le pidió a su hermano que tirara la iniciativa.
cards.grammarNote: **pidió** = he asked/requested — preterite of **pedir** (e→i stem change in él/ella and ellos forms): pedí, pediste, **pidió**, pedimos, pedisteis, **pidieron**. Other -IR e→i verbs: **servir → sirvió**, **reír → rió**, **elegir → eligió**.

cards.front:
Narrate a battle in preterite:
First… then… finally…
cards.back:
Primero, el guerrero atacó al duende.
Luego, el mago lanzó un hechizo.
Finalmente, Jeffrey derrotó al dragón con una flecha.
cards.grammarNote: Sequence markers for preterite narratives: **primero** (first), **luego / después** (then/later), **finalmente / por fin** (finally/at last). These are the building blocks of D&D storytelling in Spanish.

cards.front:
We climbed the mountain. / We climb the mountain.
(nosotros preterite vs present — -AR verbs)
cards.back:
Subimos la montaña.
(same form for both present and preterite!)
cards.grammarNote: For -AR verbs, the nosotros preterite and present are identical: **subimos** = we climb / we climbed. Context (especially time markers) determines the tense: **Ayer subimos la montaña** (Yesterday we climbed) vs **Cada día subimos la montaña** (Every day we climb).
